subject: MAT

modules.example: Solved: A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {2, 3, 4}. Union = {1, 2, 3, 4}. Intersection = {2, 3}. Method: Model run for 'Sets and relations'. Read the question and underline what is asked. Draw or write what is known. Choose the method named in the unit. Work it line by line, one idea per line, with units where they apply. Estimate first so the answer can be tested for sense. Check by working backwards. What a good answer looks like: correct method, every step visible, units stated, and a one-line check.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Use set notation, relations and functions: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Cartesian product: A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {a, b}. A x B has 3 x 2 = 6 ordered pairs: (1, a), (1, b), (2, a), (2, b), (3, a), (3, b). Order matters, so (1, a) differs from (a, 1).
Step 3, Venn counting: n(A) = 30, n(B) = 25, n(A n B) = 10. So n(A U B) = 30 + 25 - 10 = 45. Only A is 30 - 10 = 20, and only B is 25 - 10 = 15.
Step 4, Domain and range: f(x) = root of (x - 3) needs x - 3 >= 0, so the domain is x >= 3 and the range is y >= 0. For f(x) = x^2 + 1 the range is y >= 1.
Step 5, Power set: for {a, b, c}, the subsets are 2^3 = 8 in number: empty, 3 singletons, 3 pairs and the whole set. A set with n elements has 2^n subsets.
Step 6, Your turn: if n(A) = 4 and n(B) = 5 find n(A x B), and give the domain of 1/(x - 5). Answer: 20; all real numbers except 5.

modules.example: Solved: Right triangle, opposite side 3, hypotenuse 5, adjacent side 4. sin = 3/5 = 0.6, cos = 4/5 = 0.8, tan = 3/4 = 0.75. Method: Model run for 'Trigonometric functions'. Read the question and underline what is asked. Draw or write what is known. Choose the method named in the unit. Work it line by line, one idea per line, with units where they apply. Estimate first so the answer can be tested for sense. Check by working backwards. What a good answer looks like: correct method, every step visible, units stated, and a one-line check.

modules.standard: Use identities and graphs of trigonometric functions: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Radians: 150 degrees = 150 x pi/180 = 5 pi/6. And pi/4 radians = 45 degrees. The conversion factor is pi radians = 180 degrees.
Step 2, Identity: if sin x = 3/5 with x in quadrant II, then cos^2 x = 1 - 9/25 = 16/25, so cos x = -4/5 since cosine is negative there. Then tan x = -3/4.
Step 3, Compound angle: sin 75 = sin(45 + 30) = sin 45 cos 30 + cos 45 sin 30 = (root 2/2)(root 3/2) + (root 2/2)(1/2) = (root 6 + root 2)/4, about 0.966.
Step 4, Solve sin x = 1/2 for x in [0, 2 pi]: the principal angle is pi/6, and the second solution is pi - pi/6 = 5 pi/6. Check: sin(5 pi/6) = 1/2.
Step 5, Graphs: y = 2 sin x has amplitude 2 and period 2 pi, with maximum 2 at x = pi/2. y = sin 2x has period pi, so it completes one wave between 0 and pi.
Step 6, Your turn: find cos 2x when cos x = 3/5. Answer: cos 2x = 2 cos^2 x - 1 = 2 x 9/25 - 1 = -7/25.

modules.title: Principle of mathematical induction
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Principle of mathematical induction', taught in a way that is with exam-style questions and written reasoning. The target is clear: prove statements by induction. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Show it with objects or a picture: build or draw the idea in 'Principle of mathematical induction' before using symbols.
Say the rule in your own words, then write one worked line, naming each step.
Use it: prove statements by induction. Start with one easy question, then one with a real-life story.
Check it: use a second method, estimate, or work backwards to test your answer.
modules.example: Solved: Show 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1)/2. n = 1: 1 = 1. Assume it holds for k. Add k + 1: k(k + 1)/2 + (k + 1) = (k + 1)(k + 2)/2, which is the rule for k + 1. So it holds for all n. Method: Model run for 'Principle of mathematical induction'. Read the question and underline what is asked. Draw or write what is known. Choose the method named in the unit. Work it line by line, one idea per line, with units where they apply. Estimate first so the answer can be tested for sense. Check by working backwards. What a good answer looks like: correct method, every step visible, units stated, and a one-line check.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Prove statements by induction: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, State what to prove: P(n) is 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1)/2 for every natural number n. Induction works like dominoes. Show the first falls (base case), then show that if one falls the next falls (inductive step). Then all fall.
Step 2, Base case n = 1. The left side is just 1. The right side is 1 x (1 + 1) / 2 = 1. Both sides agree, so P(1) is true. Check n = 2 as well: 1 + 2 = 3 and 2 x 3 / 2 = 3.
Step 3, Inductive hypothesis: assume P(k) is true, so 1 + 2 + ... + k = k(k + 1)/2. Now add the next term k + 1 to both sides. The right side becomes k(k + 1)/2 + (k + 1).

Step 4, Simplify: k(k + 1)/2 + (k + 1) = (k + 1)(k/2 + 1) = (k + 1)(k + 2)/2. This is exactly P(k + 1), since replacing n by k + 1 gives (k + 1)(k + 2)/2. By the principle of induction, P(n) holds for all natural n. For n = 10 the sum is 55.
Step 5, Try a divisibility statement: 7^n - 1 is divisible by 6. Base: 7 - 1 = 6. Assume 7^k - 1 = 6m. Then 7^(k+1) - 1 = 7(7^k - 1) + 6 = 42m + 6 = 6(7m + 1), which is a multiple of 6.

Step 6, Your turn: prove 1^2 + 2^2 + ... + n^2 = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6. Model answer: base n = 1 gives 1 = 1 x 2 x 3/6. Assume true for k, add (k + 1)^2 to get (k + 1)(2k^2 + 7k + 6)/6 = (k + 1)(k + 2)(2k + 3)/6, which is P(k + 1).

modules.example: Solved: x squared - 5x + 6 = 0 factorises as (x - 2)(x - 3) = 0, so x = 2 or x = 3. Check x = 2: 4 - 10 + 6 = 0. Method: Model run for 'Complex numbers and quadratic equations'. Read the question and underline what is asked. Draw or write what is known. Choose the method named in the unit. Work it line by line, one idea per line, with units where they apply. Estimate first so the answer can be tested for sense. Check by working backwards. What a good answer looks like: correct method, every step visible, units stated, and a one-line check.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Operate on complex numbers and solve quadratics: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Divide complex numbers: (3 + 4i)/(1 - 2i). Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate 1 + 2i: (3 + 4i)(1 + 2i) / 5 = (3 + 6i + 4i + 8i^2)/5 = (-5 + 10i)/5 = -1 + 2i.
Step 2, Check: (-1 + 2i)(1 - 2i) = -1 + 2i + 2i - 4i^2 = -1 + 4i + 4 = 3 + 4i. This returns the numerator, so the quotient -1 + 2i is correct.
Step 3, Polar form: z = 1 + i has modulus root 2 and argument pi/4, since tan = 1 in the first quadrant. So z = root 2 (cos pi/4 + i sin pi/4). Also |3 - 4i| = 5.
Step 4, Quadratic: x^2 - 2x + 5 = 0 has D = 4 - 20 = -16. So x = (2 plus or minus 4i)/2 = 1 plus or minus 2i. The roots are conjugates, as always with real coefficients.
Step 5, Cube roots of unity: x^2 + x + 1 = 0 gives D = 1 - 4 = -3, so x = (-1 plus or minus i root 3)/2. These are the complex cube roots of 1, and their sum with 1 is 0.
Step 6, Your turn: find (2 + i)^2 and the modulus of 5 + 12i. Answer: 4 + 4i + i^2 = 3 + 4i; modulus is the root of 25 + 144 = 13.

modules.example: Solved: Arrange 5 books in 3 places: 5 x 4 x 3 = 60 ways. Choose 3 of 5: 60 / 6 = 10 ways. Method: Model run for 'Linear inequalities and permutations and combinations'. Read the question and underline what is asked. Draw or write what is known. Choose the method named in the unit. Work it line by line, one idea per line, with units where they apply. Estimate first so the answer can be tested for sense. Check by working backwards. What a good answer looks like: correct method, every step visible, units stated, and a one-line check.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Solve inequalities and count arrangements: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Solve 3x - 5 < 7: add 5 to get 3x < 12, so x < 4. On a number line, draw an open circle at 4 and shade left. Test x = 3: 9 - 5 = 4 < 7, true.
Step 2, Double inequality: -3 <= 2x + 1 < 9. Subtract 1: -4 <= 2x < 8. Divide by 2: -2 <= x < 4. So x is in [-2, 4). Test x = 0: 1 lies between -3 and 9.
Step 3, Flip rule: 4 - 3x >= 10 gives -3x >= 6. Dividing by -3 reverses the sign, so x <= -2. Test x = -3: 4 + 9 = 13 >= 10, true.
Step 4, Arrangements: 5 people in a line can be placed in 5! = 120 ways. If 2 specific people must stand together, treat them as one block: 4! x 2! = 24 x 2 = 48 ways.
Step 5, Selection: choose 4 from 6 boys and 4 girls with exactly 2 girls. C(4, 2) x C(6, 2) = 6 x 15 = 90. BANANA has 6 letters with A three times and N twice, so 6!/(3! 2!) = 60.
Step 6, Your turn: solve 5x + 2 <= 17 and find C(9, 3). Answer: 5x <= 15 so x <= 3; C(9, 3) = 9 x 8 x 7 / 6 = 84.

modules.example: Solved: 2, 5, 8, ... has a = 2 and d = 3. The 10th term = 2 + 9 x 3 = 29. The sum of 10 terms = 10/2 x (2 + 29) = 155. Method: Model run for 'Binomial theorem and sequences and series'. Read the question and underline what is asked. Draw or write what is known. Choose the method named in the unit. Work it line by line, one idea per line, with units where they apply. Estimate first so the answer can be tested for sense. Check by working backwards. modules.standard: Expand binomials and sum series: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Expand (1 + x)^4 using Pascal's row 1, 4, 6, 4, 1: 1 + 4x + 6x^2 + 4x^3 + x^4. Check x = 1: 16 and 1 + 4 + 6 + 4 + 1 = 16.
Step 2, General term: T(r+1) = C(n, r) a^(n-r) b^r. In (2 + x)^5 the coefficient of x^3 is C(5, 3) x 2^2 = 10 x 4 = 40. The third term overall has C(5, 2) = 10 as its binomial coefficient.
Step 4, GP sum: first term 3, ratio 2, 8 terms. S = 3(2^8 - 1)/(2 - 1) = 3 x 255 = 765. Check the 8th term: 3 x 128 = 384, and 765 is almost double 384, as expected for ratio 2.
Step 5, Infinite GP: 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + ... has ratio 1/2, with |r| < 1, so the sum is a/(1 - r) = 1/(1/2) = 2. When |r| is 1 or more, no such sum exists.
Step 6, Your turn: find the x^2 coefficient in (1 + 2x)^3 and the sum of 6, 2, 2/3, ... to infinity. Answer: 3 x 4 = 12; and 6/(1 - 1/3) = 9.

modules.example: Solved: Points (1, 2) and (4, 6). Distance = square root of (3 squared + 4 squared) = square root of 25 = 5. Slope = (6 - 2) / (4 - 1) = 4/3. Method: Model run for 'Straight lines and conic sections'. Read the question and underline what is asked. Draw or write what is known. Choose the method named in the unit. Work it line by line, one idea per line, with units where they apply. Estimate first so the answer can be tested for sense. Check by working backwards. modules.standard: Use equations of lines, circles and conics: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Line through (2, -1) and (5, 5): slope = 6/3 = 2. Equation y + 1 = 2(x - 2), so y = 2x - 5. Check (5, 5): 10 - 5 = 5.
Step 2, Distance from a point to a line: the distance from (1, 2) to 3x + 4y - 5 = 0 is |3 + 8 - 5| / root of 9 + 16 = 6/5 = 1.2.
Step 3, Circle: centre (3, -2) and radius 5 gives (x - 3)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 25. Test (6, 2): 9 + 16 = 25, so it lies on the circle.
Step 4, Find centre from a general equation: x^2 + y^2 - 6x + 4y - 12 = 0. Complete squares: (x - 3)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 12 + 9 + 4 = 25. Centre (3, -2), radius 5.
Step 5, Parabola y^2 = 8x: 4a = 8 so a = 2, focus (2, 0), directrix x = -2. Ellipse x^2/25 + y^2/9 = 1: a = 5, b = 3, c = root of 25 - 9 = 4, foci (plus or minus 4, 0), e = 4/5.
Step 6, Your turn: find the focus of x^2 = 12y and the radius of x^2 + y^2 = 49. Answer: 4a = 12, a = 3, focus (0, 3); radius 7.

modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Limits and derivatives, introduction', taught in a way that is with exam-style questions and written reasoning. The target is clear: find simple limits and derivatives. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.

modules.example: Solved: d/dx of (3x squared + 5x) = 6x + 5; at x = 2 the gradient is 17. Limit as x goes to 2 of (x squared - 4)/(x - 2) = limit of (x + 2) = 4. Method: Model run for 'Limits and derivatives, introduction'. Read the question and underline what is asked. Draw or write what is known. Choose the method named in the unit. Work it line by line, one idea per line, with units where they apply. Estimate first so the answer can be tested for sense. Check by working backwards. modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Find simple limits and derivatives: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Limit by factorising: lim as x approaches 2 of (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2) = lim (x + 2) = 4. Direct substitution gives 0/0, which signals the need to simplify first.
Step 2, Standard limit: lim as x approaches 0 of sin 3x / x = 3 x (sin 3x / 3x) = 3 x 1 = 3. Use the fact that sin t / t tends to 1 as t tends to 0.
Step 3, Power rule: d/dx of 5x^4 - 3x^2 + 7 = 20x^3 - 6x. The slope of y = x^3 at x = 2 is 3 x 4 = 12. The constant 7 differentiates to 0.
Step 4, First principles for f(x) = x^2: [(x + h)^2 - x^2]/h = (2xh + h^2)/h = 2x + h, which tends to 2x as h tends to 0. This confirms the power rule.
Step 5, Product rule: y = x^2 sin x. y' = 2x sin x + x^2 cos x. At x = pi/2 this is 2 x (pi/2) x 1 + 0 = pi. Compare with the quotient rule when dividing instead.
Step 6, Your turn: find the derivative of 3x^2 + 4x - 5 at x = 1, and lim of (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1) as x approaches 1. Answer: 6x + 4 = 10; the limit is x + 1 = 2.

modules.example: Solved: Data 4, 7, 7, 9, 13. Mean = 40 / 5 = 8. Median (middle value) = 7. Mode (most common) = 7. Method: Model run for 'Statistics and probability'. Read the question and underline what is asked. Draw or write what is known. Choose the method named in the unit. Work it line by line, one idea per line, with units where they apply. Estimate first so the answer can be tested for sense. Check by working backwards. What a good answer looks like: correct method, every step visible, units stated, and a one-line check.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Find variance and calculate probability: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Variance: data 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 has mean 40/8 = 5. Deviations are -3, -1, -1, -1, 0, 0, 2, 4. Squares add: 9 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 4 + 16 = 32.
Step 2, Variance = 32/8 = 4 and standard deviation = 2. So most values lie within 2 of the mean 5, between 3 and 7. Six of the eight values do, which is consistent.
Step 3, Probability of at least one head in 3 tosses: P = 1 - P(no head) = 1 - (1/2)^3 = 1 - 1/8 = 7/8. The complement method is quicker than listing 7 outcomes.
Step 4, Two dice: the sum 8 occurs as (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2), five ways out of 36, so P = 5/36. Sum at most 4 has 6 ways: P = 6/36 = 1/6.
Step 5, Exclusive and independent: for P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.5, if exclusive then P(A or B) = 0.8. If independent then P(A and B) = 0.15 and P(A or B) = 0.65.
Step 6, Your turn: find the variance of 1, 3, 5, 7, and P(sum 9) on two dice. Answer: mean 4, squares 9, 1, 1, 9 give 20/4 = 5; sum 9 has 4 ways, so 4/36 = 1/9.
